title: Why public intellectuals matter in present-day India
author: D.V. Kumar
content_html:
The term ‘public intellectual’ has an interesting origin. As Romila Thapar informs us, it was used in connection with Alfred Dreyfus, a Jewish captain in the French army who was believed to have leaked secrets to the German army. Later, it was found that he had not done anything of the kind and was declared innocent. When he was facing charges of having leaked secrets, many artists, teachers, poets and writers came together in support of him. These people came to be called public intellectuals.

A public intellectual is essentially a person who engages with the issues of the day and takes a position in support of what she believes to be true and right. She needs to raise questions about social, political and economic issues of the day using reasoned arguments so that societies would become better places to live in. A public intellectual is somebody who seeks to constantly reaffirm the foundational principles of social justice, human dignity and fraternity.

Challenging authoritarian tendencies

The role of a public intellectual perhaps has never been more critical and important than it is in the present times in India. The growing assertion of authoritarian tendencies, leading to systematic and gradual weakening of public institutions, destruction of democratic practices, silencing and, in fact criminalisation of dissent, disenfranchisement of lakhs of voters on the ground of ‘logical discrepancy’ and bulldozing of houses (especially those belonging to Muslims),’ as well as lynching of people on the grounds of storing beef in fridges and committing ‘love jihad’, are things that everybody is becoming painfully conscious of. If public intellectuals do not speak and raise their voice now, when they would do so is difficult to guess. It is their moral and ethical responsibility to speak up and stand with what is right. Silence is not a virtue in the present times. On the contrary, it can be dangerous.

Perhaps, it would be relevant to mention here what Antonio Gramsci, the celebrated Italian intellectual, wrote, ‘I hate the indifferent, also because I am annoyed by their whining as eternal innocents. I ask each of them how he carries out the role that life ordained him and daily imposes on him, what he has and especially has not done. And I feel like I can be relentless and not have to waste my pity, nor share my tears with them... I live, I am a partisan. Therefore, I hate whoever does not take sides. I hate the indifferent’. What he tried to argue was that public intellectuals should reflect and articulate their position on burning issues of the day. If they do not do so, who would do it? It is not that India has not produced great intellectuals. Starting from Buddha in the ancient India upto B.R. Ambedkar in modern times, India has had a glorious tradition of producing outstanding and powerful public intellectuals who questioned the dominant and hegemonic paradigms during their times.

Silence in academia and science

But what one finds in the present times is generalised silence from those who have the intellectual and critical faculty to be effective public intellectuals. One could refer to university teachers, poets, writers, artists and others in this regard.

A word or two about university teachers, in particular, would be in order. It is true that one need not be a university teacher to be a public intellectual, but a university teacher who is supposed to have developed critical imagination and the necessary conceptual equipment is eminently suited to be an effective public intellectual. A university teacher is expected to critically debate and articulate positions on issues of the day, however unpalatable they may be to the powers that be. But what one finds is the mysterious silence of these people on issues that are posing a severe threat to our constitutional and democratic framework. Silence is almost normalised among the university academia. If they do not write and speak on the issues concerning especially the marginalised and the weak in the society, who would do?

One may also refer to eminent scientists who could make important contributions to the debates in the society in an impartial and objective manner. Unfortunately, it is observed that they confine themselves to their narrow, specialised fields, making them disembodied and decontextualised individuals. There is a certain reluctance on their part to relate themselves to the surrounding social concerns. 

One could take a couple of examples to show what kind of contribution public intellectuals can make, if they wish to, to enrich contemporary debates. Take the example of nationalism. The way it is being constructed in the present times, there is no serious questioning of it (with very few honourable exceptions). There is no critical interrogation of the way in which Hinduism is being weaponised in terms of Hindutva. Also, attempts to convert our inclusive, democratic and civic nationalism (based on constitutional principles of equality, liberty, justice and fraternity), into exclusive, authoritarian and ethnic (Hindurashtra) nationalism are something that need to be on the top of public intellectuals’ agenda. Sadly, this is not so.

They also need to convince people that the European model of destructive, jingoistic and exclusive nationalism is not the right way to strengthen Indian nationalism, which has had a glorious history of fighting British colonialism on democratic, secular and egalitarian foundations.

Questioning fake history

Another example could be that the line between myth and history is constantly blurred, but professional historians (again with very few exceptions) have preferred to remain quiet. Academic historians are clearly not doing their job of questioning fake history (WhatsApp history) effectively. Or, for that matter, take the case of growing communalisation of public consciousness, which is essentially a tool used to divert people’s attention from issues such as unemployment, youth unrest, the unsatisfactory state of public education, price rise, agrarian crisis, etc.

There was a time when eminent scholars were invited to debates on TV channels, where they could enlighten us about many important facets of our history, culture and society. One no longer finds such debates these days. This is because either such scholars are no longer invited to debates of that kind, or they have declined to be part of debates that are now known more for their noise than for meaningful and substantive content. Anyway, one cannot really expect much from the electronic media these days, as they have allowed themselves to be commodified to an unprecedented degree.

What is thoroughly discouraged in the present times is the questioning mind. When questions are raised about the state of our polity, education, economy and society in general, they are sought to be delegitimised as anti-national and seditious, and even threats of jail are flaunted indiscriminately. Criminalisation of dissent has become normalised. But still if public intellectuals do not speak and make their presence felt now, then it will indeed be a very sad state of affairs in the country. It is true that even their most effective interventions may not result in removing oppressive structures but at least in the long run, they help in enhancing critical consciousness among the people about them.

It is in this context that one needs to appreciate the remarkable resilience shown by young protesters in the recent agitation at Jantar Mantar, in taking their fight to what they believe is its logical conclusion — the resignation of the Education Minister. One lesson that can be drawn from the largely peaceful agitation led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) is that, contrary to popular perception, the youth of the country are not a depoliticised and indifferent lot.

The large participation of young people, many of whom may have had nothing to with the NEET examination, in the protest is symbolic of their political empathy. They desired to show their solidarity, which they did. They raised a critical question of accountability, which is a basic normative feature of any democratic governance, over repeated lapses in conducting national-level examinations, and pursued it with all the might at their command.

We always underestimated the political consciousness of the country’s youth, and we need to apologise to them for this. Every act of resistance is a political act. Perhaps they have begun to play the role of a public intellectual.

(D.V. Kumar is a former Professor, Dept. of Sociology, North-Eastern Hill University, Shillong)

title: 'Gimmicks': India on Pakistan's fresh announcement on Masood Azhar bounty
author: PTI
content_html:
India on Tuesday (September 15, 2026) dismissed as "gimmicks" Pakistan's fresh announcement of a seven-million-rupee bounty on Jaish-e-Mohammed chief Masood Azhar, demanding that Islamabad take "concrete action" to combat terrorism.

Pakistan has maintained the bounty on Azhar, who continues to be listed in the country's Federal Investigation Agency's (FIA) "Red Book" of most-wanted terrorists.

Azhar remains wanted in India for major terror attacks, including the 2001 Parliament strike, the 2008 Mumbai attacks, the 2016 Pathankot airbase assault and the 2019 Pulwama bombing.

"Such gimmicks and hoodwinking by Pakistan is nothing new. We have seen similar gimmicks in the past as well," External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said at his regular media briefing, responding to a question on Pakistan maintaining the bounty on Azhar.

"For a state sponsor of terrorism to make such phoney announcements, we all know how hollow it is. Pakistan must take concrete action and not make phoney announcements. It is of no consequence," Mr. Jaiswal added.

India has for years accused Pakistan of sheltering Azhar, while Pakistan has maintained that he fled to Afghanistan - a claim rejected by Afghanistan's Taliban government.

For the last few years, Islamabad has claimed that the JeM founder has been operating from Afghanistan.

However, last week the Taliban regime dismissed Pakistan's repeated claims, with a senior Afghan Foreign Ministry official saying he is not in the country.

Islamabad's fresh announcement on the reward for information on Azhar came as it faces pressure from the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) to crack down on terror groups and their leadership.

The Paris-based global watchdog is set to review Pakistan's anti-terrorism efforts at its upcoming plenary.

Pakistan was placed under the FATF grey list between 2018 and 2022 for its systemic deficiencies in anti-money laundering and its failure to counter-terror financing.

The key reasons included its failure to curb terror financing, particularly to Jaish-e-Mohammed and Lashkar-e-Taiba terror networks, besides weak implementation of financial sanctions on UN-designated persons, people tracking FATF's actions said.

In order to exit grey listing, Pakistan was forced to take a number of steps, including banning JeM and LeT and their fronts and convicting leaders of these outfits. One of the individuals convicted in absentia in 2021 was Masood Azhar. He was designated as a global terrorist by the UN Security Council in May 2019.

In 2022, Pakistan was allowed to exit from the grey list on the condition that APG (Asia/Pacific Group on Money Laundering) would continue to review its performance on its efforts on some specific points.

One of the points on which Pakistan continues to be under review by APG on the request of FATF was its ongoing efforts to arrest Azhar.

After its exit from the grey list and a decrease in international pressure and spotlight, Pakistan has backslided on assurances it had made to FATF to exit the grey list, the people cited above said.

title: Co-location scam case: Supreme Court refuses to entertain Chitra Ramkrishna's plea challenging HC order
author: PTI
content_html:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday (September 15, 2026) refused to entertain former NSE managing director Chitra Ramkrishna's plea challenging an order taking cognisance of offences under the anti-corruption law in the co-location scam case against her.

Ms. Ramkrishna had challenged the Delhi High Court's July 9 verdict, which dismissed her plea against a trial court order taking cognisance of the offences under the anti-corruption law in the case against her.

Her plea came up for hearing before a bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran.

Senior advocate Balbir Singh, appearing for Ms. Ramkrishna, argued that the National Stock Exchange (NSE) is a private company and it can't be said that the petitioner was discharging a public duty.

While disposing of her plea, the Bench said this point could be raised before the trial court, which would consider the same on its own merits.

In its verdict, the High Court had held that the NSE performed a "public duty" and the petitioner, being its CEO and managing director, "equally performed a function and duty in which the public at large is invested".

The High Court also upheld the sanction given by the Board of Directors of the NSE to prosecute Ms. Ramkrishna, who is an accused in the co-location scam case, stating that the order was conditional to the limited extent of determination of issues pertaining to the applicability of the Prevention of Corruption (PC) Act to her, and it cannot be set aside only on this ground.

Ms. Ramkrishna had contended before the High Court that the definition of "public servant" under the PC Act was extremely vague and, therefore, was liable to be struck down.

She had also claimed that the provision cannot be made applicable to private persons employed with a private limited company.

In its judgment, the High Court stated that it did not find the definition of "public servant" under the PC Act so vague and uncertain so as to render it unconstitutional.

The High Court said that NSE is a recognised stock exchange, which is not an ordinary business venture but performs vital economic functions in the public interest, including the protection of investors, and that its shareholding is majorly in the hands of government companies.

The High Court clarified that whether the petitioner can be said to be performing a public duty in the internal management of the NSE and how far she was in charge of its day-to-day functioning and general policy decisions were matters of evidence, which cannot be determined at this stage.

The chargesheet filed by the CBI can also not be quashed by determining "such mixed questions of facts and law", it added.

The NSE co-location scam refers to the alleged abuse of the algorithm and the co-location facility by certain brokers in conspiracy with some unknown officials to make windfall profits between 2010 and 2014 when the petitioner was managing its affairs.

Ms. Ramkrishna was appointed as joint MD in 2009 and remained in the position till March 31, 2013. She was elevated to MD and CEO on April 1, 2013.

The CBI arrested Ramkrishna on March 6, 2022, in connection with the case registered in 2018. She was granted bail by the high court in September 2022.

title: Key allies TDP, Shiv Sena back Amit Shah's statement on UCC in all NDA-ruled States
author: PTI
content_html:
After Home Minister Amit Shah's assertion that a Uniform Civil Code will be implemented in all NDA-ruled States before 2029, key NDA partners TDP and Shiv Sena on Tuesday (September 15, 2026) backed the BJP on the issue.

Another BJP ally JD(U) gave a guarded response, saying it will study the Uniform Civil Code Bill and will "not oppose it for no reason".

The support of the TDP with 16 Lok Sabha MPs, the Shiv Sena with 13 and the JD(U) with 12 is crucial for the Narendra Modi government. While the TDP is in power in Andhra Pradesh along with Jana Sena and BJP, the BJP shares power with the JD(U) in Bihar and the Shiv Sena in Maharashtra.

TDP's Andhra Pradesh president P. Srinivasa Rao said in Amaravati that it is bound by the Union Home Minister's statement on UCC as an NDA partner.

"Yes, I have seen our Union Home Minister's statement on UCC and as NDA partners we are bound to go by his statement," Mr. Rao, who represents Gajuwaka assembly constituency, said.

Though there is criticism over UCC, he noted that it "strengthens the unity of the country and doesn't show much gender bias".

"And critics, of course, some say that it (UCC) infringes on religious freedom. Our country is culturally diverse. But we always think that this UCC will strengthen and unify the country," he said.

"So, we will be going by our home minister's statement being NDA partners," he added.

CPI(M) state secretary V. Srinivas Rao, however, claimed that the BJP is resorting to UCC politics to divert the country's attention as it is "facing heat from the new generation (Gen Z) due to unemployment" and other reasons, especially in the backdrop of the recent Jantar Mantar student protest movement.

Bihar Deputy Chief Minister Vijay Kumar Chaudhary also said the JD(U) will study the Uniform Civil Code Bill and will "not oppose it for no reason" if provisions are unexceptionable.

The former state JD(U) president made the statement while addressing a press conference at the party office. He was replying to queries about the political turbulence that has ensued after Shah's assertion that UCC will be implemented "across 22 NDA-ruled states by 2029".

On Monday (September 14, 2026), senior JD(U) leader and Phulwari Sharif MLA Shyam Rajak had spoken out strongly against the UCC, claiming that he was expressing a view in line with the stand taken earlier by party supremo Nitish Kumar, who had told the Narendra Modi government at the Centre, "we will support the Bill in Parliament but are opposed to its implementation in Bihar".

Mr. Chaudhary, however, maintained that "there is no reason to make haste in the matter" and pointed out that "our national working president Sanjay Kumar Jha has said that he will hold talks on the issue with none other than the Union home minister".

"As of now, we are not aware of the details of the legislation on UCC. Let it be placed before us. If we find there is nothing objectionable, why shall we oppose it without any reason? And if there are points of concern, these will be conveyed to the Union Home Minister," he said.

Maharashtra Deputy Chief Minister and Shiv Sena president Eknath Shinde backed Shah on the UCC issue, saying Sena founder late Bal Thackeray had envisioned the common law for all.

"Hinduhridaysamrat Balasaheb Thackeray's vision was 'one country, one law' with equal justice for all. Union Home Minister Amit Shah has also stated the same position on UCC," Mr. Shinde said.

He added that the Mahayuti government in Maharashtra remains positive about the Uniform Civil Code and will make a definitive decision at an appropriate time.

Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis on Monday (September 14, 2026) said the State government would implement the UCC once the committee preparing the draft bill submitted its report.

Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah said the BJP should introduce the UCC Bill in Parliament if it has the numbers to pass it, instead of pushing it through individual states, and claimed the BJP's allies also have reservations.

"If you have the numbers, bring it to Parliament. Why are you doing it through different states? Anyway, within their own NDA, not everyone agrees with this. According to the news, Janata Dal (United) raised their hands and said this won’t be implemented in Bihar,” Mr. Abdullah told reporters here.

The National Conference leader said the BJP should not bring the UCC “through the backdoor”. "The way their own allies are not in favour of it, I don’t think they will be able to get it passed in Parliament. That is perhaps why they are taking this route,” he added.

All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen (AIMIM) president Asaduddin Owaisi said in Bhopal that if the NDA constituent parties such as the JD(U) and TDP have "the slightest disagreement" with the BJP's ideology, they should oppose the Uniform Civil Code.

The UCC was being introduced in various states with the aim of "targeting" India's 18 crore Muslims, and the real objective of the BJP and RSS was to "dismantle" the protections guaranteed (to religious minorities) under Articles 25, 26, and 29 of the Constitution, he alleged.

After Home Minister Amit Shah's assertion that a Uniform Civil Code will be implemented in all NDA-ruled States before 2029, key NDA partners TDP and Shiv Sena on Tuesday (September 15, 2026) backed the BJP on the issue.
Another BJP ally JD(U) gave a guarded response, saying it will study the Uniform Civil Code Bill and will "not oppose it for no reason".
The support of the TDP with 16 Lok Sabha MPs, the Shiv Sena with 13 and the JD(U) with 12 is crucial for the Narendra Modi government. While the TDP is in power in Andhra Pradesh along with Jana Sena and BJP, the BJP shares power with the JD(U) in Bihar and the Shiv Sena in Maharashtra.
TDP's Andhra Pradesh president P. Srinivasa Rao said in Amaravati that it is bound by the Union Home Minister's statement on UCC as an NDA partner.
"Yes, I have seen our Union Home Minister's statement on UCC and as NDA partners we are bound to go by his statement," Mr. Rao, who represents Gajuwaka assembly constituency, said.
Though there is criticism over UCC, he noted that it "strengthens the unity of the country and doesn't show much gender bias".

title: Launch of expansion of Perunthalaivar Kamarajar Breakfast Scheme deferred to September 22: T.N. govt.
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
The Tamil Nadu government has deferred the launch of the expansion of the Perunthalaivar Kamarajar Breakfast Scheme, which was originally scheduled to be launched on September 17, the birth anniversary of social reformer Periyar E. V. Ramasamy, to September 22, in view of Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay’s official overseas visit to London.

In a letter to all district Collectors, Social Welfare and Women Empowerment Secretary M. Pallavi Baldev said the Chief Minister will launch the expansion of the Perunthalaivar Kamarajar Breakfast Scheme to students of Classes VI to VIII in Chennai on September 22.

On the same day, the scheme will be rolled out in all districts except Chengalpattu and Tiruppur, where the Model Code of Conduct is in force in view of the ensuing bypolls to the Madurantakam and Dharapuram Assembly segments.

Mr. Vijay, who is on his first official overseas trip to London as Chief Minister, will return to Chennai on September 17. Similarly, the State Government had already decided to defer the launch of Thaimaman Thanga Mothiram Thittam, a scheme to provide one-gram gold rings to newborns in government hospitals in the State. This scheme was originally scheduled to be launched on September 15, the birth anniversary of Dravidian stalwart and former Chief Minister C. N. Annadurai, and was subsequently deferred due to Mr. Vijay’s overseas trip.

title: Mussel and marine fish seed centre awaits commissioning as allied works drag on
author: C.P.Sajit
content_html:
The mussel and marine fish seed production centre at Puthiyangadi, Kannur, conceived as a major fisheries infrastructure project for north Keralam, is yet to be commissioned as specialised allied works remain incomplete even though the main civil construction has been completed.

The ₹5-crore project, conceived during the first Pinarayi Vijayan government, was planned as the State’s first dedicated hatchery for mussel and marine fish seed production, with an annual production capacity of 50 lakh marine fish seeds and 50 lakh mussel seeds. The delay in completing the remaining works has kept the facility from becoming operational.

The modern modular hatchery has been equipped for mussel seed and marine fish seed production with a live feed production unit, algal culture unit, larval rearing tanks, a recirculating aquaculture system for fighting fish conservation and seed production, and a laboratory. The infrastructure includes a 1,208.6-square-metre hatchery building, a 133-metre drainage system, 30-tonne capacity FRP tanks, blowers, ozonators, rapid and slow sand filters, and specialised plumbing and electrification systems for continuous operation.

R. Jugnu, Deputy Director of Fisheries, Kannur, said the civil works had been completed, but some specialised works inside the facility, particularly the installation of tanks and related systems, were still pending.

She attributed the delay partly to difficulty in finding contractors willing to undertake the specialised works. “It is a new type of hatchery, and there are specialised works involved. There was an issue as people were not coming forward to take up the tender,” Ms. Jugnu said.

The project is being implemented by the Kerala State Coastal Area Development Corporation (KSCADC) with technical assistance from the Central Marine Fisheries Research Institute (CMFRI).

KSCADC Regional Manager Ashique Babu said the agency had completed works worth around ₹3 crore under the original contract, while additional works costing more than ₹1 crore now remained to be executed.

He said repeated attempts to tender some of the additional works had initially failed to attract contractors. A contractor has now taken up the work, allowing the second phase to proceed.

“Some additional civil works have to be done outside the building. New plumbing arrangements are required to bring seawater to the facility. There are also ponds to be constructed outside the building and a greenhouse to be set up. In addition, new seawater filtration systems and some more tanks have to be installed,” he said.

The centre is particularly important for Kannur and Kasaragod, the two major mussel culture districts in north Keralam. There is currently no comparable hatchery in the northern zone, and farmers largely depend on the wild collection of mussel seeds.

According to Ms. Jugnu, the dependence on wild seed often creates conflicts between mussel cultivators and fishermen. Seed availability also varies considerably according to natural conditions.

“At present, seed is collected from natural habitats and transported from areas, including Kozhikode and Malappuram, where availability is comparatively higher. A 50 kg sack of mussel seed has recently cost around ₹3,500 to ₹4,000, while prices have reached as high as ₹10,000 in years when wild seed availability was low,” she said

Kannur and Kasaragod are the two major districts where mussel culture is practised. “At present, we collect the seed from the wild, and this often leads to conflict. The hatchery is expected to provide a dependable source of quality seed and reduce dependence on wild collection. This would also help ease the competition over natural seed resources,” Ms. Jugnu said.

She further said that mussel culture is mainly undertaken from October to March. During the remaining months, the facility can be used to produce seed of other marine species, allowing the infrastructure to be utilised throughout the year.

The centre is also expected to reduce farmers’ dependence on seed brought from outside the region and provide a more predictable supply for aquaculture activities. The involvement of CMFRI is expected to provide scientific support for hatchery operations, quality control and conservation practices.

With the principal civil work complete, the immediate challenge is the execution of the remaining specialised components. The completion of these works and the commissioning of the centre are expected to provide north Keralam with a dedicated facility for the scientific production of mussel and marine fish seed and reduce the sector’s reliance on the availability of wild seed.

title: Monkeys, wild boars emerge as major sources of human-wildlife conflict in Wayanad
author: C.P.Sajit
content_html:
Monkeys and wild boars, rather than elephants and tigers, are emerging as the most persistent sources of human-wildlife conflict in Wayanad, according to a three-year scientific study jointly conducted by researchers from Kannur University and the University of Geneva.

Conducted across 49 villages and involving 998 respondents, the study found that 84% had experienced conflict with wildlife, while 81% held negative perceptions towards wildlife conservation. All the villages reported interactions with wildlife.

The research was led by Joseph J. Erinjeri, Assistant Professor, Department of Zoology, Mananthavady Campus, Kannur University, and researcher Lakshmi C.M. of the Department of Zoology, Kannur University, along with Takuyu Iwamura of the University of Geneva. Former Professor of Zoology P.K. Prasadan, research scholar Stefina C.C. of Kannur University, and Tanner Corless Smith of the University of Geneva were part of the team.

The study has been published in Scientific Reports, a Q1 journal in the Nature Portfolio published by Springer Nature.

Conflict reported in all 49 villages

According to Mr. Erinjeri, eight species were identified as the principal sources of conflict — monkeys, wild boars, elephants, tigers, leopards, gaurs, deer, and peafowl.

He said monkeys accounted for the highest proportion of reported interactions, followed by wild boars. Peafowl were reported by around 30% of respondents, elephants by 23%, and deer by 17%. Encounters with tigers, gaurs, and leopards were less common, accounting for 4%, 3%, and 3%, respectively.

“The study found that people’s perception of wildlife was influenced not merely by the species encountered, but also by the number of species, frequency of their visits, and the intensity of the resulting conflict,” he said.

Monkeys, wild boars cause repeated losses

Mr. Erinjeri said monkeys and wild boars caused the greatest day-to-day disruption. Around 37% of respondents rated conflict with monkeys as moderate to high in severity, compared with 31% for wild boars.

Monkey-related conflicts recorded the highest proportion of extreme severity responses. Around 5% of respondents placed them in the extreme category, citing crop and property damage. For all other species, the proportion reporting extreme conflict was below 1.5%.

Wild boars were particularly associated with agricultural losses. Around 30% of respondents rated conflict with them as very high in severity, mainly because of extensive crop damage.

The researchers said repeated losses caused by smaller animals can impose a substantial cumulative burden on farming communities, even if individual incidents receive less attention than attacks by large mammals.

According to researchers, elephant encounters were reported by 23% of respondents. Though less frequent than interactions with monkeys and wild boars, they had greater implications for property, crops, livelihoods, and human safety. Around 11% rated elephant conflict as very high in severity and 1% as extreme.

Mr. Erinjeri said interactions with tigers and leopards were rare, but generated disproportionate fear. Respondents reporting attacks on livestock or domestic animals involving these carnivores recorded extreme levels of conflict.

“The findings suggest that the frequency of encounters alone cannot determine their impact. While monkeys and wild boars caused repeated disruption, large carnivores posed serious safety concerns even when encounters were infrequent,” he said.

Distance from forest does not determine severity

The researchers also examined forest distance and the severity of wildlife conflict. The relationship was found to vary between species, indicating that proximity to forest alone does not explain the intensity of human-wildlife interactions.

Call for a broader compensation framework

The researchers said wildlife management strategies should consider the frequency, geographical spread, and the cumulative impact of conflict. Compensation mechanisms, they added, should cover repeated crop damage caused by monkeys and wild boars and not focus only on high-profile incidents involving elephants and large carnivores.

Zoonotic disease transmission under study

The research team is now pursuing further studies on the possibility of zoonotic disease transmission associated with increasing wildlife movement into human settlements and the encroachment of humans and livestock towards forest boundaries.

“Research into zoonotic disease transmission associated with movement of wildlife into human settlements, as well as the movement of humans and livestock towards forest boundaries, is currently under way in our laboratory,” said Mr. Erinjeri.

The researchers said species-specific and location-specific approaches would be essential to address the increasingly complex human-wildlife interactions in the Western Ghats.
